Alex — thanks again for the demo today. Quick recap and a proposed lightweight testing plan so we can move from qualitative evaluation to a head-to-head unit-econ comparison.

Recap (very high level)
- Halliday use case: high-concurrency chat summarization + occasional long-context retrieval (~avg prompt 350–600 tokens, ~20% long-context >2k tokens).
- Key constraints you called out: p50 latency target <= 250ms, cost < $8 / 1M generated tokens for production inference, and encryption-in-flight needs are non-negotiable.

Redwood differentiators to frame the probe
- Routing by SLO: we can route latency-sensitive traffic to smaller-batched low-latency pools and cheaper throughput to quantized pools automatically.
- Prefix/KV caching: for repeated context (session state + retrieval keys) we expect 30–70% effective cache hit rates depending on your prompt reuse.
- Cost controls: batching + cache policies usually change effective per-1M token unit cost by 2–3x depending on hit rate and sequence length.

Proposed comparative test matrix (what we suggest Redwood run vs your hyperscaler baseline):
1) Baseline: 1M tokens, batch sizes [1, 8, 32], cache-hit rates [0%, 50%, 80%] — measure cost-per-1M, p50/p95 latency, and GPU occupancy.
2) Long-context variant: run 200k tokens with average context 2k tokens to capture KV-cache and memory pressure effects.
3) Mixed concurrency: 1k concurrent streams at avg prompt 450 tokens to validate autoscale and steady-state cost.

What we need from Halliday (to make the comparatives apples-to-apples):
- A 24–48 hour sample trace (timestamps + prompt/response sizes). The sample helps us pick sequence-length distributions.
- Target p50/p95 SLOs for each route (we can suggest defaults).

Deliverables we will commit to for the probe (initial):
- A short-run report with measured cost per 1M tokens under the matrix above (Redwood hosted, Redwood quantized pool, and a comparable hyperscaler config).
- CSV with raw request logs + cost model assumptions.
- Recommendations: batching/cache knobs to reduce unit cost to target.

Timeline proposal: kickoff Mon 11/30, data handoff by Tue 12/1, bench run Wed–Thu, deliverable Fri 12/4. Flexible if you need more time.

Attachments: halliday-usage-sample.csv (if you can export a 48hr slice that’s perfect).

Next: if that plan looks good, can you confirm the sample availability and preferred SLOs? Happy to sync 30-min if you want to walk through the matrix.

—

Alex — received, thanks for the trace. I sketched a quick sanity calc with the halliday sample and a couple of assumptions to set expectations before we run full benches. High level numbers (very approximate) below — we’ll replace with measured figures after the bench: 

Assumptions used for the sketch
- Redwood hosted LLM (optimized fp16, continuous batching): nominal baseline generation cost ~ $4.20 / 1M tokens at batch size 8 and cache 0%.
- Optimized quantized pool (dedicated reserved): nominal generation cost ~ $2.10 / 1M tokens at batch size 32 and cache 70% (effective).
- Hyperscaler comparable config (what you reported + our validation): ~ $12.50 / 1M tokens at batch size 16 and cache 0% (their managed service, generic instance class).

Illustrative deltas from the matrix (per-1M generated tokens)
- Batch sensitivity (holding cache=0%): batch=1 -> 3.6x higher than batch=32; batch=8 is ~1.4x of batch=32 for the same model on our runtime.
- Cache sensitivity (holding batch=8): going from 0% -> 50% cache hits reduces effective spend by ~38%; 0% -> 80% reduces by ~58% (because cached prefixes avoid model decode).

Net: For your sample distribution we expect the realistic production range to be $1.8 — $6.5 / 1M tokens depending on routing (latency-priority vs cost-priority) and cache hit rate. That contrasts with your quoted current baseline of ~$13 / 1M.

Proposed immediate next step (low effort):
- We run the 3x3 grid (batch sizes 1/8/32 x cache 0/50/80) for 1M tokens on your sample shape, measure p50/p95 and cost, and share the CSV. This will make the numbers concrete.

Do you want Redwood to run the hyperscaler baseline in the same test harness (we can spin up a comparable managed endpoint and run the same replay) or would you prefer to run that side and share results? Running both sides from our harness speeds up the apples-to-apples comparison.

I’ll draft a short statement for procurement with the range and assumptions; Rishi & Grace are looped to scope the bench.

—
Lauren
